input.command: ls -la; cat src/ci.ts; grep -rn "getBuild\|fetch\|timeout\|AbortSignal" --include=*.ts --include=*.js --include=*.json . | grep -v node_modules | head -50
cat package.json; sed -n 1,80p src/routes.ts; ls src; grep -rn "timeout\|setTimeout\|signal\|server\|listen" src | head -30

input.reason: In src/ci.ts:4, getBuild calls `fetch(`${CI}/builds/${id}`)` with no options: no `signal`, no AbortController, and no AbortSignal.timeout. I searched src/ for timeout, setTimeout, signal and server/listen setup and found none. The only caller, the `build` route in src/routes.ts:52, awaits getBuild directly with no timeout or race. Nothing in the repository limits how long this outbound request can take. One mitigation applies: on Node, the built-in fetch (undici) has default headers and body timeouts of about 300 seconds. So under Node the request fails after about five minutes instead of hanging forever. That lowers the impact, but the claim stands: the code sets no timeout of its own, and a stalled CI endpoint holds every /build request open for minutes. On a runtime without those defaults, it can hold them open with no limit.

evidence.code: no matches: no timeout or abort signal is configured anywhere in src/

input.failure_scenario: ci.example.com accepts the TCP connection but stops responding. Each request to the `build` route (src/routes.ts:52) then waits inside getBuild's fetch (src/ci.ts:4). On Node that wait lasts until undici's roughly 300-second default timeout. On other runtimes it may never end. While the CI server stays stalled, callers pile up with open requests and held resources, and none of them gets a timely error.
input.severity_reason: This is a real reliability risk, but it only shows up when the external CI service stalls. On Node, undici's default timeouts of about 300 seconds limit the wait, so it is not an unbounded hang or an outage in normal use. That fits Medium better than High.
